pages.text: Every Thursday, the Letter Club met in the corner classroom. On the wall hung a big chart of a friendly letter, with each part in a different coloured box. “A letter,” said Madam Frimpomaa, “is a conversation on paper. Today we are going to build one together, part by part.” Kwasi Cobbinah picked up his pen. He was writing to his cousin Doreen in Cape Coast.
sentences: Every Thursday, the Letter Club met in the corner classroom.
On the wall hung a big chart of a friendly letter, with each part in a different coloured box.
“A letter,” said Madam Frimpomaa, “is a conversation on paper.
Today we are going to build one together, part by part.” Kwasi Cobbinah picked up his pen.
He was writing to his cousin Doreen in Cape Coast.
pages.alt: A teacher stands beside a chart of a letter with coloured boxes while students hold pens.

pages.text: Part one: the address and date. “In the top corner of the page, left or right,” said Madam Frimpomaa. “Write your own address, not your friend’s. Under it, write the date.” Kwasi wrote: House 12, Palm Street, Koforidua. Beneath it: 14th May, 2027. “Notice there are no chat-style numbers or short forms,” said Hannah. “Full month, full year.”
sentences: Part one: the address and date.
“In the top corner of the page, left or right,” said Madam Frimpomaa.
“Write your own address, not your friend’s.
Under it, write the date.” Kwasi wrote: House 12, Palm Street, Koforidua.
Beneath it: 14th May, 2027.
“Notice there are no chat-style numbers or short forms,” said Hannah.
“Full month, full year.”
pages.alt: A student writes an address and date in the top right-hand corner of a page.

pages.text: Part two: the greeting. “Dear Doreen,” wrote Kwasi. “A comma after the name,” said Madam Frimpomaa. “And a capital letter for every name.” Part three: the opening. “Begin warmly. Ask after health or say why you are writing.” Kwasi wrote: “I hope this letter finds you and everyone at home in good health. I am writing to tell you about our school Letter Club.”
sentences: Part two: the greeting.
“Dear Doreen,” wrote Kwasi.
“A comma after the name,” said Madam Frimpomaa.
“And a capital letter for every name.” Part three: the opening.
“Begin warmly.
Ask after health or say why you are writing.” Kwasi wrote: “I hope this letter finds you and everyone at home in good health.
I am writing to tell you about our school Letter Club.”
pages.alt: A student writes a greeting and the first lines of a letter, with a teacher pointing to the comma.

pages.text: Part four: the body. “This is the heart,” said Madam Frimpomaa. “One paragraph for each main idea. Give details: who, what, where, when, how. Use linking words such as firstly, however, because and finally. And remember, you are talking to a cousin, so you may be warm and friendly, but you are still writing in full words and correct spelling.”

“This is the heart,” said Madam Frimpomaa.
“One paragraph for each main idea.
Give details: who, what, where, when, how.
Use linking words such as firstly, however, because and finally.
And remember, you are talking to a cousin, so you may be warm and friendly, but you are still writing in full words and correct spelling.”
pages.alt: A teacher points to the body of the letter chart, with paragraph boxes and linking words listed beside it.

pages.text: Kwasi wrote about the Letter Club, about the day Hannah put a full stop in the middle of a sentence and about Madam Frimpomaa’s red pen. “You may be funny in a letter,” said Madam Frimpomaa, “but be funny in words, not in abbreviations. ‘I laughed until my sides ached’ is much better than ‘lol’. It paints a picture the marker can see.”
sentences: Kwasi wrote about the Letter Club, about the day Hannah put a full stop in the middle of a sentence and about Madam Frimpomaa’s red pen.
“You may be funny in a letter,” said Madam Frimpomaa, “but be funny in words, not in abbreviations.
‘I laughed until my sides ached’ is much better than ‘lol’.
It paints a picture the marker can see.”
pages.alt: Students laugh in a classroom while a teacher waves a red pen playfully.

pages.text: Part five: the closing paragraph. “Wrap up and look ahead,” said Madam Frimpomaa. Kwasi wrote: “I must stop here because it is time for supper. Please write back and tell me about your new school.” Part six: the sign-off. “Yours ever, Kwasi.” “Or ‘Your loving cousin’, ‘Your friend’, ‘Yours lovingly’,” said Hannah. “For a friend or relative, any warm closing is fine.”

“Wrap up and look ahead,” said Madam Frimpomaa.
Kwasi wrote: “I must stop here because it is time for supper.
Please write back and tell me about your new school.” Part six: the sign-off.
“Yours ever, Kwasi.” “Or ‘Your loving cousin’, ‘Your friend’, ‘Yours lovingly’,” said Hannah.
“For a friend or relative, any warm closing is fine.”
pages.alt: A student writes the closing lines and sign-off at the bottom of a page.

pages.text: Madam Frimpomaa gave the class a checklist. Did I write my address and the date? Did I use “Dear” and a comma? Did I open warmly? Did I write in paragraphs with details? Did I use full words and correct spelling? Did I close warmly and sign off? “Check your letter against this list,” she said, “and you will not lose silly marks.”
sentences: Madam Frimpomaa gave the class a checklist.
Did I write my address and the date?
Did I use “Dear” and a comma?
Did I open warmly?
Did I write in paragraphs with details?
Did I use full words and correct spelling?
Did I close warmly and sign off?
“Check your letter against this list,” she said, “and you will not lose silly marks.”
pages.alt: A checklist with six tick boxes pinned on a board beside the letter chart.

pages.text: Kwasi posted his letter, and two weeks later Doreen wrote back. “Dear Kwasi, what a wonderful letter! You wrote so clearly that I could picture the Letter Club.” Kwasi grinned. “A good letter,” he told Hannah, “is a hug on paper. And a good exam letter,” said Hannah, “is a hug with a checklist.” The end.
